title: Computer Eyes 👁️

mascot.name: Chip
mascot.greeting: Hi, it's Chip! How does a phone know it's your face? Let's look at pictures the way a computer does!

recap: To a computer, a picture is a grid of numbers.
A small window slides over the picture to find edges.
Stacks of filters find lines, then shapes, then things.

sections.heading: 1. Pictures Made of Tiny Squares
sections.bigIdea: To a computer, every picture is a grid of numbers.
sections.chipQuote: Zoom in really close on a photo. What do you see?

analogy.description: A mosaic is a picture made of little tiles. Up close you see tiles. Step back, and you see a face.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Zoom in on a photo, and you will see tiny squares called **pixels**. Each pixel is one colour.

A computer can't see colours the way you do. It turns each pixel into a number. Dark pixels get small numbers. Bright pixels get big numbers. So a photo is a big grid of numbers.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: The tiny coloured squares that make up a picture on a screen.

diagram.caption: From photo to numbers
diagram.alt: Three steps: a photo is made of tiny squares, each square gets a number, and the whole photo becomes a grid of numbers.
steps: A photo is made of tiny squares. 🟦🟦
Each square gets a number. Dark is small, bright is big.
The whole photo becomes a grid of numbers. 🔢

more.title: Which numbers?
more.bodyMarkdown: In a black and white picture, black is often 0 and white is 255. All the greys are in between.

teen.add: A colour pixel has three numbers: how much red, green and blue it has. Mix those three, and you can make any colour on a screen.

checkIn.question: What does a computer turn each pixel into?
checkIn.explanation: A computer turns every pixel into a number.

sections.heading: 2. The Sliding Window
sections.bigIdea: A small window slides over the picture to find edges.
sections.chipQuote: I look at a picture one small patch at a time!

analogy.description: You slide a magnifying glass over a map, one spot at a time, looking for rivers.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
To find shapes, the computer uses a tiny window called a **filter**. It is only three squares wide.

The filter slides across the picture, one step at a time. At each stop, it checks the numbers under it. Where dark meets bright, it lights up. That line is an **edge**.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: A tiny window that slides over a picture looking for one kind of pattern.
A place in a picture where dark meets bright, like the outline of a shape.

diagram.caption: How the sliding window works
diagram.alt: Four steps: the window sits on one patch, checks its numbers, lights up if dark meets bright, and then slides one step on.
steps: The window sits on one small patch. 🔍
It checks the numbers under it.
Dark next to bright? It lights up! ✨
It slides one step and checks again. ➡️

teen.add: This slide-multiply-add trick is called **convolution**. The numbers inside the filter decide what it finds: edges, blur or lines in one direction.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: Sliding a filter over a picture and adding up what it finds at each spot.

interactiveWidget.title: 🔍 Try It: The Edge Finder
interactiveWidget.instruction: Pick a drawing and a filter. Watch the glowing squares show where the edges are.
interactiveWidget.goal: Make the computer light up the edges of a shape.
interactiveWidget.predictionPrompt: Before you pick a filter: where do you think the edges are?
hints: Edges are where dark meets bright.
Try the blur filter to see the opposite.
interactiveWidget.successMessage: Edges found! That is the first thing computer eyes learn to see.

sections.heading: 3. From Lines to Faces
sections.bigIdea: Stack lots of filters, and the computer sees bigger and bigger shapes.
sections.chipQuote: Lines make shapes. Shapes make things!

analogy.description: Small blocks make a wall. Walls make a room. Rooms make a whole house.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
One filter finds simple lines. Now stack lots of filters in rows. The first row finds lines. The next row joins lines into shapes, like circles. The last row joins shapes into things, like a cat's face.

The computer learns which filters to use by itself, from lots of photos.

diagram.caption: Each row sees something bigger
diagram.content:
graph LR
    P["🖼️ Photo"] --> L1["Row 1: lines ➖"]
    L1 --> L2["Row 2: shapes ⭕"]
    L2 --> L3["Row 3: things 🐱"]
diagram.alt: A photo goes into row 1, which finds lines, then row 2, which finds shapes, then row 3, which finds things like a cat.

teen.add: A stack like this is called a **convolutional neural network**, or CNN. Each row is a layer, just like the layers of neurons in lesson 3.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: Layers of filters that find lines, then shapes, then whole things. Also called a CNN.

checkIn.question: What does the first row of filters find?
checkIn.praise: Right! The first row finds lines.
checkIn.explanation: The first row finds lines. Later rows join them into shapes and things.

sections.heading: 4. Computer Eyes All Around You
sections.bigIdea: Computer eyes help us every day.
sections.chipQuote: Cameras plus AI can spot things super fast!

analogy.description: A camera can watch all day and night without getting tired or bored.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Your phone uses computer eyes to open when it sees your face. Cars use them to spot people crossing the road. Doctors use them to look at X-rays. Farmers use them to spot sick plants.

But computer eyes can make mistakes. For big choices, a person still checks.

diagram.caption: Where computer eyes help
diagram.content:
graph TD
    V["👁️ Computer eyes"] --> A["📱 Face unlock"]
    V --> B["🚗 Spotting people on the road"]
    V --> C["🩻 Checking X-rays"]
    V --> D["🌱 Finding sick plants"]
diagram.alt: Computer eyes help with face unlock, spotting people on the road, checking X-rays and finding sick plants.

teen.add: Computer eyes only know what they were shown. If a face camera learned from too few kinds of faces, it can fail for some people. You will see why in lesson 7.

checkIn.question: Who should check a big choice made with computer eyes?
checkIn.praise: Yes! People check the big choices.
checkIn.explanation: Computer eyes can make mistakes, so a person checks big choices.

miniQuiz.question: What is a picture to a computer?
miniQuiz.explanation: A computer turns each pixel into a number, so a picture is a grid of numbers.

miniQuiz.question: What does the sliding window light up?
miniQuiz.explanation: The filter lights up where dark meets bright. That is an edge.

miniQuiz.question: What does the first row of filters find?
miniQuiz.explanation: The first row finds lines. Later rows find shapes, then things.

miniQuiz.question: What is a stack of filter layers called?
miniQuiz.praise: Exactly! Stacks of filters make a CNN.
miniQuiz.explanation: Layers of filters that find lines, shapes and things are called a convolutional neural network.

teachBack.prompt: Chip asks: How does a computer find a cat in a photo? Pick the best answer for a friend.
options: It turns the photo into numbers and finds lines, then shapes, then the cat.
It looks at the photo just like a person does.
Someone tells it where the cat is every time.
teachBack.explanation: Right! Numbers, then lines, then shapes, then the cat.

recall.question: What does a weight do in a neuron?
options: It says how much a clue counts
recall.explanation: A weight says how much each clue counts.
